title: Reading the heading
hookLine: a track title tells you the song and the artist before you press play; so does the line above each hymn
tomorrow: a hymn has many lines. which one do you read first?

cards: A song comes up in a playlist and before you press play, the screen has already told you things: the title, the artist, maybe that it's live or acoustic. You know the voice and the feel before the first note.
Open the Granth to almost any hymn and there's the same kind of line above it, in smaller print. It isn't a title. It's for the ear.
It tells you how this hymn should sound, and whose voice you're about to hear.

teach.h: FIRST, THE RAGA: HOW IT FEELS.
teach.b: Read the heading left to right and it gives up three things. First, the raga: the musical mode the hymn is set in, with its own mood. Asa, Sorath, Bilaval.
Before you know what the hymn says, you know how it should feel.

teach.h: MAHALA AND A NUMBER: WHOSE VOICE.
teach.b: Second, Mahala and a number: whose voice this is. Every Guru signs as Nanak inside the hymns, so the heading does the naming. Mahala one is Guru Nanak; Mahala five is Guru Arjan.
Third, sometimes, the word ghar and a number.
And here's the honest part: scholars differ on exactly what ghar told the musicians, a beat, a scale, a style. The Granth gives the label and doesn't explain it.
At the start of a new section, the heading may also carry Ik Onkar, Satgur prasad: the One, reached by the Guru's grace. So here's the thing worth telling someone tonight.
The Granth tells you how a hymn should sound, and whose voice it is, before it gives you a single word.
The words arrive already dressed in a mood.

how: In the Guru Granth Sahib each hymn sits under a heading naming its raga and its author by Mahala number, sometimes with a ghar; kirtan singers sing the hymn in the raga its heading names.

games.q: a friend opens the Granth to a hymn headed Asa, Mahala 5. she asks who wrote it and how it's meant to sound. what does the heading tell her?
o: the raga Asa sets the feel, and Mahala 5 is Guru Arjan's voice.
it's Guru Nanak's hymn, since the hymn itself is signed Nanak.
the hymn is called Asa, and this page is its fifth verse.
games.why: the heading names the raga first, then the Guru by Mahala number: five is Guru Arjan. the signature Nanak sits inside the hymn; the heading does the naming.

practice: Find three headings, in a gutka, a printed copy or an app. For each one, say the raga's name out loud, and tap the Mahala number on your knee, one tap for Guru Nanak, five for Guru Arjan.
Then rest your hands, breathe, and let the last raga's name sound once more in your head, like a note held after the music stops.

wordCard.voice: Reading the heading: the small line above each hymn, naming its raga, the Guru's voice by Mahala and number, and sometimes its ghar. The sixth word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Mahala, the word in a heading that, with a number, names which Guru's voice the hymn is.

carryVoice: For the road: the heading tells you how it sounds and whose voice it is, before the first word. Six of twenty, heard.

sources.ref: hymn headings throughout the raga sections (from Sri Raag, Ang 14 on): raga, Mahala and number, and sometimes ghar; section openings with Ik Onkar, Satgur prasad
